title: Characters of Clay
tagline: He invented movable type four centuries before Gutenberg.

scenes.text: China, Song Dynasty, ~1040 CE. Bi Sheng, a craftsman, stares at a block of clay. He has an idea that will change the world — though the world won't know his name for centuries.
He carves individual characters into clay tiles, fires them hard, and arranges them in an iron frame. Movable type: each character reusable, reconfigurable — infinite books from finite pieces.

challenge.instruction: The characters are carved and fired hard. Slide the clay type into reading order inside the iron frame, the way Bi Sheng set a page.
challenge.fact: Bi Sheng invented movable type during the Song Dynasty (c.1040 CE) using baked clay — the same material Chinese potters had mastered for thousands of years. Each character was carved in clay, hardened by fire, then set in an iron frame with pine resin. After printing, the resin was heated and the characters removed for reuse.

scenes.text: He tests the process methodically — two frames allow one to print while the other is set. Speed doubles. His innovation is also a system.

challenge.instruction: Fire turns soft clay into type that will not soften again. Balance the reactions of Bi Sheng’s kiln and plate: the same atoms must leave as went in.
challenge.fact: Despite its ingenuity, Bi Sheng's clay type did not replace woodblock printing, which remained dominant in China for centuries. Chinese has tens of thousands of characters, making movable type logistically complex — a single print job might require thousands of individual pieces. Woodblock printing remained faster for short texts. Movable type proved more revolutionary in alphabetic languages like Korean and later European languages.

scenes.text: The Chinese writing system's thousands of characters make movable type harder than in alphabetic scripts — but Bi Sheng organizes them by rhyme category for fast retrieval.

params.title: Counting the Type
params.intro: A page needs many copies of the commonest characters. Add each count the compositor calls out on the counting frame and press Enter — the beads must show the running total.
params.fact: Shen Kuo says Bi Sheng made several pieces of type for every character, and more than twenty for common ones such as 之 and 也, so they could appear many times on one page. A rare character was carved and fired on the spot.

challenge.instruction: Thousands of characters wait in cases labelled by rhyme. Tally how many pieces of the commonest ones the next page will need.
challenge.fact: Bi Sheng's system was described in detail by the statesman Shen Kuo in his 'Dream Pool Essays' (1088 CE) — one of the great scientific documents of the medieval world. Without Shen Kuo's account, we might never have known of Bi Sheng's invention, since none of his actual type survives.

scenes.text: We know about Bi Sheng only because the polymath Shen Kuo recorded his invention decades later. Bi Sheng himself left no writings — just the type blocks, and the idea.

challenge.instruction: Bi Sheng hardened his type in fire, as Song potters hardened their wares. Glaze each band of the vase with the right oxide, then fire the kiln.
challenge.fact: Song Dynasty China (960–1279 CE) was a civilization of extraordinary technological creativity: compass navigation, gunpowder weapons, paper money, paddlewheel ships, and movable type all emerged in a single century. The Song state funded scientific investigation and published encyclopedias — creating the world's first information economy.

scenes.text: Gutenberg's press came 400 years later. But the concept — movable, reusable type — was first pressed into clay by an artisan in Song Dynasty China.

challenge.instruction: Shen Kuo, who recorded Bi Sheng’s type, also recorded a spring that turned iron pans to copper. Use the reactivity series to make the salt you are asked for.
challenge.fact: Writing had been recorded on clay tablets since Mesopotamia in 3500 BCE. Bi Sheng's great insight was that clay — the oldest writing substrate in human history — could itself become the tool for mass reproduction of text. He connected the ancient world of clay and the modern world of print in a single creative act.

scenes.speaker: Bi Sheng
scenes.text: Ibn Battuta waits at Changan, but nothing is happening there, and without an event there is no fight. I will go first; the turn after I arrive, play the Argument card on Changan and we attack.

challenge.fact: Event cards start a scenario at a location where you already have a Great Person, and only one who arrived on an earlier turn can start it. A local event keeps running until a player ends it.
